title: Lesson 3 - A1.2.2 Hacking
subject: Information Technology
bigQuestion: How does hacking threaten data and what are the consequences?

sections.heading: What is hacking?
sections.text: Hacking is gaining unauthorised access to a computer system, network or data without the owner's permission. Anyone, from large multinational companies to individuals, can be a victim.
points: Used to steal sensitive information, disrupt services, alter data, or take control of systems
Targets businesses, government organisations and individuals
Example: the 2017 Equifax data breach exposed the personal information of millions of people after hackers got into company systems
Example: the M&S cyber attack (covered by BBC News) took down services such as digital click & collect

sections.heading: Data theft
sections.text: Hackers often get into systems to steal confidential information.
points: They may COPY the data, so the victim doesn't even know they've been hacked
Or they may REMOVE it from the system completely, to cause maximum damage and disruption
Taking data and threatening the victim with it is known as double extortion

sections.heading: Data tampering
sections.text: Instead of stealing data, a hacker might change it for someone's benefit or to cause damage.

head: Type
What is changed
Examples
rows: Back-end tampering
Databases and other data stores behind the scenes
Changing personal or financial details for personal gain; making big changes so a system stops working properly
Front-end tampering
The appearance of a website or other public-facing information
Defacing a website as a prank, or taking it over and demanding a ransom to restore it

sections.heading: DoS and DDoS attacks
points: DoS (denial of service): an attack designed to shut down a network. One machine, often a web server, is flooded with traffic so it stops working properly or crashes
DDoS (distributed denial of service): a large-scale, co-ordinated attack from a network of computers
In a DDoS, hackers spread bots across many compromised computers
The infected computers ('zombies') flood the target with requests from many different locations at once

head: DoS
DDoS
rows: Where it comes from
One machine, using a script or tool
Many infected machines (bots) in a botnet, run by a command-and-control (C&C) server
Detection and stopping it
Easier: one source, so the connection can be cut. A good firewall can do this
Harder: comes from many remote locations, which disguises its origin
Tracing the source
Easier to trace
Much harder, because of the botnet
Speed
Slower to deploy
Faster to deploy, so harder to spot in time: more damage, possibly catastrophic
Traffic volume
Limited to one machine's traffic
Huge amounts of traffic at once, overloading the server rapidly

sections.heading: Browser hijacking for hacking
sections.text: A browser hijacker can be used to steal confidential data such as usernames and passwords.
points: Browsers often save usernames and passwords
Hackers can use these to get into accounts: banking, shopping and streaming services
Link to Lesson 2: hijackers also change your homepage and search engine and redirect you to malicious sites

sections.heading: Cyber warfare
sections.text: Organisations, governments and countries hacking each other to access secret information, and blocking each other's attempts to hack them.

head: Type
What it is
Motivation
rows: Espionage
Spying on another country's or organisation's systems to steal secrets
Gain a military, political or economic advantage
Sabotage
Attacking systems to damage or disrupt them, e.g. government or military systems
Weaken an enemy and disrupt their operations
Economic
Attacking banks, financial systems or businesses
Damage another country's economy
Infrastructure
Attacking essential services such as power, water, transport and communications
Cause widespread disruption, danger and panic

head: Victim
Possible consequences
rows: Businesses
Services go down and sales are lost; customer data stolen; damaged reputation and trust; ransom demands; possible fines
Governments
Secret information stolen; public services disrupted; risks to national security and critical infrastructure
Individuals
Personal and financial details stolen; accounts accessed with saved or stolen passwords; identity theft and fraud

keyIdea: Hacking is unauthorised access to systems or data. Hackers steal data, tamper with it, knock services offline with DoS and DDoS attacks, or hijack browsers to grab passwords, and the consequences hit businesses, governments and individuals.
flashcards: Hacking
Gaining unauthorised access to a computer system, network or data without the owner's permission.
Unauthorised access
Getting into a system or data you don't have permission to use.
Data theft
Stealing confidential information, either by copying it (victim may not notice) or removing it completely.
Double extortion
Hackers take data and use it against the victim, e.g. threatening to sell or leak it as well as disrupting systems.
Data tampering
Changing data instead of stealing it, for someone's benefit or to cause damage.
Back-end data tampering
Editing databases or data stores, e.g. changing financial details or breaking how a system works.
Front-end data tampering
Changing how a website or public display looks, e.g. defacing it as a prank or for ransom.
DoS attack
Denial of service: one machine floods a target, often a web server, with traffic so it stops working or crashes.
DDoS attack
Distributed denial of service: many infected computers flood a target at once from many locations.
Bot / zombie
An infected computer secretly controlled by a hacker and used in attacks such as DDoS.
Botnet
A network of bots used together for a large-scale attack.
Command-and-control (C&C) server
The server a hacker uses to control the bots in a botnet.
Why DDoS is harder to stop
It comes from many locations, which disguises its origin, so you can't just block one source.
Firewall vs DoS
Because a DoS comes from one location, a good firewall can detect it and cut the connection.
Traffic volume (DDoS)
Many bots send far more traffic at once, overloading a server rapidly.
Browser hijacker (hacking)
Used to steal usernames and passwords, including ones saved in the browser.
Saved passwords risk
Passwords saved in a browser can be used by hackers to get into banking, shopping and streaming accounts.
Cyber warfare
Organisations, governments and countries hacking each other for secret information and blocking each other's attacks.
Cyber espionage
Spying on systems to steal secrets for a military, political or economic advantage.
Cyber sabotage
Attacking systems to damage or disrupt an enemy's operations.
Economic cyber warfare
Attacking banks, financial systems or businesses to damage another country's economy.
Infrastructure attack
Targeting essential services like power, water, transport or communications to cause widespread disruption.
Equifax (2017)
Data breach that exposed the personal information of millions of people after hackers got into company systems.
M&S cyber attack
Attack that took down M&S services such as digital click & collect, shown in the BBC News report on the slides.

o: Gaining unauthorised access to a computer system, network or data
quiz.e: Hacking is getting into systems or data without the owner's permission.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a DoS and a DDoS attack?
o: A DDoS comes from many computers at once; a DoS comes from one
A DoS is always more powerful
quiz.e: The extra D is for 'distributed': many infected computers attack together.

quiz.q: Which is something hackers might do after gaining access?
o: Report the weakness to the police
quiz.e: Once inside, hackers may steal data, tamper with it, disrupt services or take control of systems.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a DDoS attack?
o: To flood a target with traffic so it slows down, stops working or crashes
quiz.e: DDoS attacks overload a target, often a web server, so legitimate users can't use it.

quiz.q: A hacker copies a company's customer list but leaves the original in place. Why might they do this?
o: So the victim doesn't know they've been hacked
To fix errors in the data
quiz.e: Copying data can go unnoticed, so the hacker can use or sell it without the victim reacting.

quiz.q: A hacker changes the bank details stored in a company's payroll database. What is this?
quiz.e: Editing databases and data stores behind the scenes is back-end tampering.

quiz.q: A council's website homepage is replaced with a joke message. What is this?
quiz.e: Changing the public-facing appearance of a website is front-end tampering.

quiz.q: Why is a DoS attack easier to stop than a DDoS attack?
o: It comes from one location, so the connection can be cut, e.g. by a firewall
quiz.e: One source is easy to identify and block. A DDoS comes from many places, disguising its origin.

quiz.q: In a DDoS attack, what controls the botnet?
quiz.e: The hacker uses a C&C server to co-ordinate all the infected machines.

quiz.q: Why can a DDoS attack overload a server so quickly?
o: Many bots send huge amounts of traffic at the same time
quiz.e: Lots of machines attacking at once means huge traffic volume, very quickly.

quiz.q: How can a browser hijacker help a hacker get into someone's bank account?
o: It mails them the bank card
It changes the bank's interest rate
It uses usernames and passwords saved in the browser
quiz.e: Browsers often save login details, which a hijacker can steal and use.

quiz.q: Countries hacking each other to access secret information is called:
quiz.e: Cyber warfare includes espionage, sabotage, economic attacks and infrastructure attacks.

quiz.q: An attack on a country's power grid that causes blackouts is an example of:
quiz.e: Attacks on essential services like power, water and transport are infrastructure attacks.

quiz.q: How can data tampering affect an organisation?
o: It has no effect if nothing is stolen
Wrong data can stop systems working, cause financial loss and damage trust
quiz.e: Changed data can break systems, lead to wrong decisions or payments, and damage reputation.

quiz.q: Which is a difference between front-end and back-end tampering?
o: Front-end changes what the public sees; back-end changes the data stores behind it
Back-end is only done by accident
quiz.e: Front-end = public appearance (e.g. a website). Back-end = databases and data stores.

quiz.q: Who can be a victim of hacking?
o: Anyone, from multinational companies to individuals
quiz.e: Businesses, governments and individuals are all targets.

apply.title: Name that attack
apply.intro: Read each situation and pick the attack or the best answer. In the exam, always link your answer to the scenario.

items.task: An online shop's website crashes after being flooded with requests from thousands of computers around the world.
items.e: Thousands of computers in many locations = distributed denial of service.

items.task: A small website crashes after one computer sends it a huge stream of requests. The IT team blocks that one address and it stops.
items.e: One source that can be blocked = DoS.

items.task: A hacker quietly copies a company's customer database and later sells it online. The company doesn't notice for months.
items.e: Copying data so the victim doesn't notice, then selling it, is data theft.

items.task: Students' exam grades in a school database are secretly changed.
items.e: Changing data in a database is back-end tampering.

items.task: A football club's website is replaced with a message saying 'Pay us £10,000 to get your site back'.
items.e: Changing the public-facing site and demanding a ransom to restore it is front-end tampering.

items.task: After installing a free toolbar, someone's streaming and shopping accounts are logged into from another country.
items.e: Hijackers can grab usernames and passwords saved in the browser.

items.task: One country hacks another country's defence ministry to read secret military plans.
items.e: Spying to steal secrets is espionage.

items.task: Hackers backed by a foreign state shut down a nation's water treatment systems.
items.e: Attacking essential services such as water is an infrastructure attack.

items.task: A country's banks and stock exchange are attacked to damage its economy.
items.e: Targeting financial systems to harm an economy is economic cyber warfare.

items.task: The IT team can't work out where a website attack is coming from, because traffic arrives from thousands of different addresses. Why?
o: The attack uses a botnet, which disguises its origin
The website has no domain name
items.e: In a DDoS, bots in many locations hide the real source, making tracing much harder.

items.task: Hackers take a company's files off its system completely and threaten to release them unless they're paid.
items.e: Taking data and using it to pressure the victim is described on the slides as double extortion.

items.task: A shop's click & collect service stops working after a cyber attack, and customers can't collect orders. Who is affected?
o: The business (lost sales and reputation) and its customers
items.e: Like the M&S attack: the business loses money and trust, and customers can't get their orders.

pts: Gaining unauthorised access to a computer system, network or data
without the permission of the owner
exam.tip: Two marks = two parts: what (unauthorised access) and the condition (without permission).

exam.q: 2. Give one example of what a hacker might do after gaining access to a system.
pts: Any one: steal data; tamper with/change data; delete data; disrupt services; take control of the system; sell the data

exam.q: 3. State the main purpose of a DDoS attack.
pts: To flood a target (e.g. a web server) with traffic so it slows down, stops working or crashes
exam.tip: Keep it short: overload the target so it can't work.

exam.q: 4. Describe one difference between front-end and back-end data tampering.
pts: Front-end tampering changes the appearance of a website or public-facing information
whereas back-end tampering changes the data stored in databases or other data stores
exam.tip: Describe BOTH sides. "Whereas" links them neatly.

exam.q: 5. Explain how data tampering could affect an organisation.
pts: Changed data could be wrong or stop a system working properly
so the organisation could lose money, make wrong decisions or payments, and lose customers' trust

exam.q: 6. Describe two types of cyber warfare.
pts: Type 1 named, e.g. espionage
Description, e.g. spying on another country's systems to steal secret information for an advantage
Type 2 named, e.g. sabotage / economic / infrastructure
Description, e.g. damaging enemy systems / attacking banks to harm the economy / attacking power or water supplies
exam.tip: Name each type, then say what it is or why it's done.

exam.sc: Pennine Outdoor sells camping gear through its website and three shops. Its customer database holds names, addresses, card details and order history. Staff log in to the admin systems using passwords saved in their web browsers. Last month the website went offline for six hours after being flooded with traffic from thousands of computers around the world.
exam.q: 7. Identify the type of attack that took Pennine Outdoor's website offline.
pts: DDoS (distributed denial of service) attack
exam.tip: The clue is "thousands of computers around the world": that makes it distributed.

exam.sc: Pennine Outdoor sells camping gear through its website and three shops. Its customer database holds names, addresses, card details and order history. Staff log in to the admin systems using passwords saved in their web browsers. Last month the website went offline for six hours after being flooded with traffic from thousands of computers around the world.
exam.q: 8. Explain why the attack on Pennine Outdoor's website was harder to stop than a DoS attack from one computer.
pts: The traffic came from thousands of computers (a botnet) in many locations
so the origin was disguised and couldn't be blocked by cutting one connection or using a firewall
Many bots sent huge amounts of traffic at the same time
so the server was overloaded rapidly and the attack was harder to detect in time
exam.tip: Two points, each with a reason. Use the slide's comparison: source, tracing, speed, volume.

exam.sc: Pennine Outdoor sells camping gear through its website and three shops. Its customer database holds names, addresses, card details and order history. Staff log in to the admin systems using passwords saved in their web browsers. Last month the website went offline for six hours after being flooded with traffic from thousands of computers around the world.
exam.q: 9. Explain how a browser hijacker could be used to steal data from Pennine Outdoor.
pts: A browser hijacker is installed on a staff member's web browser
It steals the usernames and passwords saved in the browser
so the hacker can log in to the admin systems and steal the customer database (names, addresses, card details)
exam.tip: Use the scenario: staff save their passwords in the browser. That's the weakness.

exam.sc: Pennine Outdoor sells camping gear through its website and three shops. Its customer database holds names, addresses, card details and order history. Staff log in to the admin systems using passwords saved in their web browsers. Last month the website went offline for six hours after being flooded with traffic from thousands of computers around the world.
exam.q: 10. Assess the impact a hacking attack could have on Pennine Outdoor and its customers.
pts: Impact on the business: lost sales while the website is down (e.g. the six-hour outage)
Impact on the business: stolen or tampered customer data damages reputation and trust, and could lead to fines or a ransom demand
Impact on customers: names, addresses and card details could be stolen and sold
Impact on customers: risk of fraud and identity theft, and accounts being accessed
Weighs up which impact is most serious (e.g. data theft lasts longer than a few hours of downtime)
Justified conclusion linked to the scenario
exam.tip: Top-grade "assess" = cover BOTH the business and customers, compare how serious each impact is, and finish with a clear judgement.
